review:
I would recommend only getting this if you've got some good friends to hop in with. I'll start with the positives and get to the negatives of the game, then again this is early access.

Positives:
Engaging puzzles
Good atmosphere
Great concept
Plenty of variety

Negatives:
The A.I. is shotty at times, more specifically in some scenarios you end up "pinned" for a good while
The graphics are passable at best, and the effects of insanity make it unplayable, then again I feel as if that's the point

The VR:
This gets it's own section as it largely soured my view of the game. VR is insanely shotty and the insanity isn't properly ported, meaning if you're insane the motion blur is enough to give you a headache, combine that with the janky VR mapping and goofy player models, it's fun for an hour on VR but inevitably desktop is the golden standard for this game.
Overall?
I'd only recommend it if you're playing with some friends and enjoy puzzle games, otherwise it'll be a difficult experience, and VR is heavily not recommended.

I’m a long-time player of Inside the Backrooms. First of all, thank you for making such a unique horror game.

The overall progression and routes were changed.
Many puzzles were removed or altered.
The difficulty was significantly reduced compared to the old version.
I understand that games need to evolve, but I really miss the old map design, level flow, puzzle style, and the original difficulty. I also know many other veteran players feel the same way.

Could you please consider adding a Classic Mode / Legacy Mode that keeps the old maps, old progression, old puzzles, and the original difficulty? That way new players can enjoy the new content, while old players can still play the version we fell in love with.

If keeping the old content in the game isn’t possible, it would also be great if you could provide a way to roll back to the previous version, for example through a Steam beta branch.

Thank you again for your work, and I hope you’ll consider the feedback from long-time players.

Best regards,

Inside the Backrooms: The Definitive Puzzle-Based Horror Experience
Having spent countless hours in this game and even unlocked all the achievements before new ones were added, I can confidently say that Inside the Backrooms is absolutely worth buying. It stands out from other games in the genre by focusing on a more methodical, puzzle-solving approach that's both challenging and incredibly rewarding.

This game is a breath of fresh air for those who want more than just running from monsters. The puzzles are complex and well-designed, requiring you to think and work with your teammates to progress. While the core experience is less reliant on jump-scares compared to a game like Escape the Backrooms, the entities themselves are still a massive threat, and the tension of being hunted is palpable. It’s easy to get lost in the game’s deep, unsettling levels, which is a good thing since this game offers a substantial experience that will take you a long time to beat.

Pros
Challenging and Rewarding Puzzles: The puzzles are a core mechanic that sets this game apart and makes it feel incredibly unique.

Effective Horror: The entities are a genuine threat that will make you jump if you're not paying attention.

Substantial Gameplay: With a lengthy campaign and a lot to discover, this game offers excellent value.

Cons
Less Terrifying Atmosphere: The game's tone is more unsettling than outright terrifying, especially when compared to the relentless scares of a game like Escape the Backrooms.

Small Player Community: Finding a public match can be a challenge, so you'll want to bring some friends along to get the full experience.

Final Score
9/10

Inside The Backrooms takes you on a thrilling journey through the eerie layers of the Backrooms. It's a short yet satisfying horror game that captures the essence of the creepypasta lore. But there are a few things we wish we knew before delving into this spine-chilling adventure.

Stamina is a crucial factor, and running around recklessly will quickly drain it, leaving you vulnerable. Respawning is possible, but the door's location changes each time, so don't waste time searching for the same spot. Losing your flashlight means navigating in the dark or finding a replacement, as items don't respawn. 

Puzzles are randomly generated, adding replayability and keeping you on your toes.  Entities in the game may not follow the exact rules from the lore, so don't rely solely on your prior knowledge. The game's order of levels also deviates from the canon, offering a fresh experience. Beware of the birthday party section, as it presents the toughest challenge in the game by far. 

Lastly, while the ending may not be as satisfying as the rest of the game, it's still a worthwhile journey.

Inside the Backrooms is a psychological horror and survival co-op game that takes the increasingly popular mythos of the Backrooms and turns it into a tense, puzzle-laden nightmare that thrives on atmosphere, teamwork, and dread. Built around the concept of players being trapped in a distorted, infinite maze of liminal spaces filled with eerie silence, flickering lights, and cryptic threats, the game excels at immersing players in its unsettling world while forcing them to rely on each other for survival. Whether played solo or with up to four friends, Inside the Backrooms manages to evoke a creeping fear not just from jump scares, but from the slow-burn anxiety of being watched, lost, or hunted in a place that feels wrong on a fundamental level.

Gameplay revolves around navigating a series of interconnected rooms and levels, each more confusing and dangerous than the last. The environments are bleak, sterile, and oppressively empty—until they’re not. Strange noises, shifting shadows, and cryptic entities begin to appear, some passive, some deadly. The game doesn’t hold your hand; you’re forced to learn through trial and error. Progress requires solving puzzles, managing stamina, and avoiding or escaping mysterious creatures that inhabit the backrooms. These entities aren’t just obstacles—they’re manifestations of the unknown, and the game cleverly uses audio cues, subtle environmental changes, and timing to keep players constantly second-guessing themselves. Death is frequent and often sudden, but it rarely feels cheap.

One of the game's most distinctive strengths is its focus on cooperation. Playing with others adds a layer of tension and urgency to every decision. Communicating over voice chat becomes essential—not only for coordinating puzzle-solving but for calling out threats and guiding lost teammates. When someone goes silent, you immediately wonder: did they get disconnected, or did something find them? The cooperative element makes Inside the Backrooms more than just a survival horror experience—it becomes a shared psychological test, heightening the fear through emotional investment and group dynamics. No one wants to be the last one left alive, wandering the endless corridors alone.

The puzzles themselves are surprisingly robust, ranging from straightforward code-breaking to environmental pattern recognition and memory challenges. Often, the information you need is scattered across rooms, requiring the team to split up, share findings, and sometimes risk exposure to hostile entities. While some puzzles can feel obtuse on the first attempt, they are generally fair and satisfying to solve, especially under pressure. Inventory management and item use also play roles, and while the mechanics are relatively simple, they’re effective in creating a sense of urgency when navigating dangerous zones or preparing for the next big encounter.

Visually, the game leans heavily on its liminal design principles. The fluorescent-lit office spaces, beige hallways, and untextured ceilings all contribute to an uncanny sense of familiarity warped into terror. It doesn’t rely on grotesque imagery as much as psychological unease. The minimalist aesthetic, paired with effective lighting and a truly oppressive sound design, makes for a chilling atmosphere that gets under your skin. The screeching noises of nearby monsters, flickering lights during tense moments, or just the heavy silence broken by a teammate’s panicked breathing all combine to build an experience that’s more about dread than outright horror.

That said, the game is not without flaws. As an indie title, some technical limitations are apparent. Movement can feel clunky, animations are sometimes stiff, and occasional bugs can interrupt immersion. Difficulty balancing can be uneven as well—some levels are incredibly punishing, while others feel underwhelming. Players new to the Backrooms concept or unfamiliar with its meta-horror themes may also feel lost, as the game provides little narrative context beyond the bare minimum. Despite these shortcomings, the frequent updates and active development show the developers' dedication to polishing and expanding the experience.

Inside the Backrooms is a strong example of minimalist horror done right. It captures the surreal, disorienting essence of its source material and transforms it into an interactive test of nerves, logic, and teamwork. The combination of fear-driven exploration, cooperative gameplay, and high-stakes puzzle-solving makes for a unique and memorable horror experience. Whether you’re a veteran of the Backrooms lore or just discovering the genre, this game will leave you unsettled long after you’ve logged out, wondering what might still be lurking just around the corner of an empty hallway.

this game contains the most tedious unenjoyable puzzles that lead to a payoff that does not feel rewarding at all. near the end, the only sense of pleasure i got once i complete a level is the knowledge that it is finally over. i walk at the pace of a lethargic handicapped american citizen, and i have the stamina bar to match. aesthetically and atmospherically the first three levels are great, with unique environments that keep the game refreshing. once you reach the sewers, the game loses that atmosphere and you're met with enemies placed and paths crafted in the most inconvenient ways in order to pad out the game's playtime. the enemies aren't scary in the slightest, and are moreso just an inconvenience designed to stall out your objectives as much as possible. mechanically, the game tries in many ways but fails in even more. whenever a player dies, they drop all items on the ground and must pick them up once they respawn. this becomes very tedious in the long run, especially if a player forgets to pick up their items. overall the concept of the game is good, but every one of those concepts is executed in a way that feels unpolished and designed to drag out the experience as much as possible which leads to a boring experience. the game also has a few technical problems, with the AI being horrible and VR being nearly unplayable due to many features not  being updated for VR. if you're looking for a good backrooms experience, there are many games that pull it off better in every way.

A very unpolished version of the backrooms, there are only a couple of monsters present in the game and they themselves are not special in any way. The game itself is very stretched, the mechanic used is that areas that should be counted as chapters are not saved, game is only saved when you finish the entire chapter, so there could be 4 difficult parts in it and the game would only be saved after doing all 4 of them, that is because if it was saved after every major area, the game would be extremely short maybe 1 max 1 hour and 30 minutes, so the developer tried to create an illusion of a lengthy game simply by not saving areas and forcing players to do an entire chapter in order to be saved.

That is a very poor excuse, considering the price is very similar to Escape The Backrooms coop game, which itself is very well done, has many different chapters and the game itself is quite unique, this however is not, at all. If you have extra cash to spare, you can buy it, but if you want a good experience of the backrooms in coop, buy Escape the Backrooms, that game is an experience you wont forget, in a good way. This game: inside the backrooms wont be a worthy to remember experience, so it should not be on top of your list.

Maybe the game will become better, with more unique chapters, less stretching of length and upgraded save mechanics, but what it is right now, I can not recommend it at all.
